• Common name: Monte Carlo
  • Other names: New Large Pearl Grass, Bacopita
  • Scientific name: Micranthemum tweedei
  • Lighting: medium to high
  • Substrate: needed
  • Growth rate: moderate
  • Placement: mostly foreground / midground
  • Height: 3–6 cm
  • CO2: not needed – low
  • Propagation: splitting, cutting off daughter plants

Choose healthy plants without spots or rips in the leaves. Tissue culture or nursery plants are both available. Quarantine new plants before adding them: they can carry parasites, snails or predators such as dragonfly and damselfly nymphs, or be treated with pesticides that are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

Monte Carlo is named after the city of Monte Carlo in Misiones Province, north-eastern Argentina, where Japanese collectors found specimens on a riverside. It is called "Bacopita" in South America, and "Monte Carlo" or "New Large Pearl Grass" by most hobbyists.

This plant is found on riversides, marshes and the banks of streams and rivers in South America. It is well adapted to nano, medium or large tanks.

Description: vibrant light green colour, small structure, round leaves of 5–10 mm, height of 2–5 cm, long filiform creeping stems, small axillary solitary flowers with very short stalks, long tiny roots, and stems/runners that form dense mats or carpets.

Monte Carlo is a carpet plant and can easily cover a large area of the tank. It suits nano tanks, with a minimum tank size of 20 litres. More is better: 40–80 litres accommodates the plant and other inhabitants properly.

Planting: 1–2 pots are enough for a 20–40 litre tank. Tissue culture is free of algae and pests. For tissue culture: remove the plant from its container, rinse off the nutrient gel, split it into 8–10 small pieces, and use tweezers to push each piece deep into the substrate. For nursery plants: remove the pot, detach the rock wool and rinse off any particles from the roots, then split and plant as above. If plants pop out, keep wedging them back in; they will eventually root. The Dry Start Method also works.

Carpet: With too little light the plant grows tall towards the light and is less dense; more light makes it greener and denser. A nutrient-rich substrate helps. Trim regularly so new side shoots form and the carpet becomes compact. Be patient.

Maintenance: A compact carpet takes about 4–8 weeks to form. With strong light and adequate CO2 it grows fast and needs trimming about every 2 weeks. Use sharp curved scissors with long handles, trim from the top down to a few centimetres above the ground, and sieve out floating cuttings to avoid dirt and excess ammonia. Without trimming, light cannot reach the base, which rots, turns brown and may die. Remove dead plants gently.

Problems:

  • Melting: high nitrite causes melting after planting; change water.
  • Brown stems: light does not reach the base; trim regularly.
  • Yellowing and slow growth: when the carpet is thicker than 4–5 cm. Cut it back to 2–3 cm; keeping it at 3–4 cm is better.
  • Poor attachment: wedge the plant back in deep enough to root.
Keep the temperature at 20–25°C and the pH at 6.0–7.5, measuring regularly to keep it stable. The plant appreciates water hardness up to 15 GH and tolerates a wide range of hardness.

Lighting: Monte Carlo needs moderate to high light; it can survive under low light, but that is not suitable. Substrate: it thrives in a fine or small-grained, nutrient-rich soil substrate, such as Caribsea Eco-Complete, Seachem Fluorite Black Sand, Fluval Stratum or ADA Amazonia.

Supplements: external fertilisation and CO2 are not mandatory, but they help the plant grow faster and more compact. Injecting CO2 and using a liquid fertiliser such as Seachem Flourish is advisable.

Monte Carlo can be grown with stem plants such as Rotala indica, Water Wisteria, Italian Val and AR Mini. It does well with shrimp and non-aggressive fish such as clown loach, mollies, neon tetras, cardinal tetras and rasboras. It provides cover for fry and shrimp.
